lessons.title: நாய், பூனை — solid ground to close the arc, and an honest three-way split
lessons.gloss: dog and cat — நாய் is THE solid, ancient, undisputed Dravidian root behind Kannada/Malayalam's dog-words too, the honest opposite of the tangled dog-words of Spanish, Hindi, and English; பூனை is Tamil's everyday cat-word, one of (at least) three genuinely separate Dravidian cat-word families

segments.text: This whole ANIMALS arc kept finding mystery dog-words — Spanish's perro, English's dog, Hindi's kuttā, each one an unsolved puzzle displacing an older, expected word. Tamil's dog-word closes the arc on the complete opposite footing: total, undisputed solid ground.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: நாய் — no mystery, anywhere

segments.text: நாய் (nāy, "dog") is a solid, native Proto-Dravidian root — the exact same one behind Kannada's ನಾಯಿ (nāyi) and Malayalam's നായ (nāya). There is no debate about its origin, no substrate mystery, nothing like the perro/dog/kuttā pattern that ran through Spanish, English, and Hindi. Three unrelated language families each lost their expected word for "dog" to an unexplained newcomer — and right here, in the Dravidian family, the expected word simply survived, plainly and solidly, across (at least) three of its languages.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart - பூனை — Tamil's word, and an honest three-way Dravidian split

segments.text: பூனை (pūnai, "cat") is Tamil's own everyday word, matching Malayalam's പൂച്ച (pūcha) closely — but be honest that "cat" splits Dravidian in a way "dog" doesn't. Kannada's everyday word, ಬೆಕ್ಕು (bekku), comes from a different ancient root (related to the word for "wildcat"); Telugu's, పిల్లి (pilli), comes from yet another separate Proto-Dravidian root, most likely the very source behind Sanskrit's biḍāla and Hindi's billī. Tamil itself even keeps rarer, alternate cat-words — பில்லி and வெருகு — cognate with Telugu's and Kannada's everyday choices respectively, showing that all three roots were once available across the family; each language just settled on a different one as its everyday word.

segments.instruction: the honest split — Kannada's bekku and Telugu's pilli come from two other, separate ancient roots
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the honest split — Kannada's bekku and Telugu's pilli come from two other, separate ancient roots]

segments.text: Is நாய் a mystery word, like Spanish's perro, English's dog, or Hindi's kuttā? (No — a solid, undisputed native Dravidian root, shared with Kannada and Malayalam.) Does பூனை share a root with Kannada's bekku or Telugu's pilli? (No — all three are genuinely separate ancient Dravidian roots; Tamil even keeps rarer alternate cat-words, pilli and veruku, echoing both of them.) Which Dravidian cat-word is most likely the source of Sanskrit's biḍāla and Hindi's billī? (Telugu's pilli.)

lessons.title: என் (eṉ) — the third vowel that opens a word
lessons.gloss: a third word-initial vowel, reached by a rule you already had

waitUntilStopped: Script you'll notice: build the word
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: எ and Script you'll notice: build the word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: You know the rule already: a Tamil word that opens on a vowel opens with a full vowel letter, never a sign. You have seen it twice — ஆ in ām, இ in illai. Here is the third, in a word you have been saying since chapter 2.
எ is the independent letter for short e. Same job as ஆ and இ, one more vowel along.

Three words, three different vowels, one rule doing the work each time. That is what makes the rule worth having: you did not need to be told about எ separately, only that word-initial vowels get a full letter.
Read எ; do not draw it yet. This book gives a stroke order only where it has a sourced one, and எ does not have one yet.

blocks.title: Script you'll notice: build the word

utterances: piece: எ, e, independent — the word opens on a vowel.
piece: ன், bare ṉ — ன under a puḷḷi, the alveolar n, from நன்றி.

segments.text: Two pieces, and you have met both halves before: the alveolar ன is the middle one of Tamil's three n's, and the dot on top is the same puḷḷi that closes வணக்கம்.

segments.instruction: ஆம், இல்லை, என் (eṉ) — three words, three opening vowels
segments.source: [YOU CONTRAST: **ஆம்** · **இல்லை** · **என்** — three words, three opening vowels]

segments.text: Read என் (eṉ). Why does it open with a full எ rather than a sign? (The word starts on a vowel — there is no consonant to hook onto.) Which vowel opens இல்லை? (இ.) What is the dot doing on ன்? (Removing the built-in a, leaving a bare ṉ.) Next: green and yellow, and a colour word the whole Dravidian family shares.
